questions.q: A handler contains const body = request.body as RefundBody;. What does the as RefundBody part do when the program runs?
questions.explain: A type assertion is a promise to the compiler, and types are erased when TypeScript compiles to JavaScript. At runtime the body is whatever the client sent. Only runtime validation (a schema or a hand-written check) looks at the actual value.
options: It checks the body's shape and throws if it does not match
It converts the body's fields to the declared types
Nothing: it only tells the compiler to treat the value as a RefundBody, and is removed from the JavaScript
It removes fields that are not in RefundBody

questions.q: A customer sends a perfectly well-formed refund request for their own order, with a valid session. Support staff should approve refunds, not customers. Which layer must stop this request?
questions.explain: The request is well-formed, so the schema accepts it, and the compiler never sees runtime data at all. Only a security control that knows who the caller is (from the session) and what they may do can refuse it.
options: The authorization check, using the role from the server-side session

questions.q: Which of these problems can TypeScript's type checker catch on its own?
questions.explain: Types protect developers from mistakes in the source code they write. Everything that arrives while the program runs (requests, rows, files, environment variables) is invisible to the compiler and needs runtime checks.
options: A client sending "4500000" (text) as the amount
Your own code calling refund(amountKobo, orderId) with the arguments in the wrong order
A customer claiming to be a manager
A database row written by an older version of the code, with a missing column

questions.q: Where should a refund handler get the caller's role from?
questions.explain: The caller writes the whole request: body, headers and query. Validating a role field only proves it is one of the allowed words, not that it is true. The role is a fact the server knows, so it comes from the server's session store or database.
options: A role field in the JSON body, validated with z.enum
The server's own session record (or verified token), looked up from the session token
A query-string parameter, because it is logged

questions.q: A refund schema uses z.strictObject, so a body with an extra role field gets 400. With z.object the field would be silently dropped. Why does the lesson prefer rejecting it?
questions.explain: With either schema, later code only sees the parsed result, which has no role. Rejecting makes the unexpected field visible: a client bug gets fixed, and repeated attempts to send fields like role show up in your logs.
options: Dropping unknown fields is unsafe, because they stay in the parsed result
Both keep the field out of later code, but rejecting also tells you about clients that are confused or probing
Zod cannot infer a type from z.object

questions.q: A profile update does await db.users.update(actor.userId, { ...body }) after checking that body.name is a string. What is the risk?
questions.explain: Checking one field says nothing about the others. Spreading the raw body copies every key the client chose into the update. Build the update from the parsed result of a strict schema, or from an explicit list of allowed fields.
options: The spread operator is slow on large objects
Any other field in the body (for example a role or balance column) is written to the row too: mass assignment
The user id could be changed by the body

questions.q: Which version follows "parse, don't validate"?
questions.explain: In A the check runs, but the original body is what gets saved, including anything the schema would have stripped or transformed (trimmed strings, defaults, removed keys). B passes on only what the schema produced, and needs no as.
options: A, because it checks before saving
B, because it uses the new object the schema built, not the original body

questions.q: A new role "intern" is added to the Role type, but nobody updates the rule. Which function keeps interns from approving refunds?
questions.explain: B lists who is allowed and denies everything else, so an unknown role fails closed. A lists who is refused and allows the rest, so every new role is allowed until someone remembers to add it.

questions.q: Functions take a branded OrderId that only OrderId.parse creates. Which line in a route file quietly defeats that protection?
questions.explain: An as cast creates the brand without running the check, so the type says "validated" about a value nobody validated. Keep brand-creating casts inside the schema module and treat any other one as a review finding.

questions.q: Why does the lesson's Secret class store the value in #value instead of a TypeScript private value property?
questions.explain: TypeScript's private is erased like every other type annotation. A JavaScript # field is enforced by the engine: it is not a property, so generic code that walks an object's properties never sees it. Neither encrypts anything.
options: They are identical; # is just shorter
private is only a compile-time rule, so the value is still an ordinary property that Object.keys, spreading and printing can see; #value is a real private field
private properties cannot be read by methods of the class

questions.q: A logger calls JSON.stringify on a configuration object that contains a Secret three levels deep. Why is "[redacted]" logged?
questions.explain: The protection is on the value itself, so it works wherever the value ends up, without every logger having to know about it.
options: The logger searches for keys named key or secret
JSON.stringify calls toJSON() on every object it meets, at any depth, and the Secret returns "[redacted]"

questions.q: In which order should a refund handler run its steps?
questions.explain: Identity first, so unauthenticated callers do no work; then a well-formed request; then the server's own data about the object; then the decision, which needs all of these; and only then the action, followed by the audit record.
options: Validate the body, act, then check the session
Authorize using the body, validate, then authenticate
Authenticate (session), validate the body, load the order, authorize, act, record
Load the order, act, then authorize in a background job

questions.q: A customer asks for GET /orders/ORD-2001, which belongs to another customer. What should the response usually be?
questions.explain: Answering 403 confirms that the order exists, which lets someone discover valid order numbers. For objects whose existence is private, "not allowed" and "not found" should look the same to the caller. Log the real reason on the server.
options: 200 with the fields the customer may see
404, the same as for an order that does not exist

questions.q: Why does the lesson's 400 response list the names of the fields that failed, and not the values that were sent?
questions.explain: The field name is enough for a client to fix the request. Copying raw input into responses (and logs) is how injection reaches pages and how passwords end up in log files.
options: Values are too long to send back
Echoing input back into responses can turn into reflected XSS and can repeat sensitive data; the client already knows what it sent
Zod does not keep the values
HTTP forbids request data in error responses

questions.q: What does putting .max(500) on every string field of a request schema protect against?
questions.explain: Limits bound the cost of one request. They work together with a body size limit that is checked before JSON.parse runs; the schema's limits cannot help if a 500 MB body has already been parsed.
options: A single request costing a large amount of processing, storage or memory
Nothing, because JSON strings have a built-in limit

questions.q: The refund reason passed the schema (3 to 500 characters). It is later shown on an admin web page. What else is needed?
questions.explain: Validation says the value is well-formed, not that it is safe in every destination. Each destination has its own defence: HTML encoding for pages, parameters for SQL, argument arrays for programs. Stripping punctuation would also damage legitimate text.
options: A stricter regex that removes all punctuation
Encoding for HTML where it is written into the page
Storing it as a branded type

questions.q: const data = await response.json(); gives data the type any. What is the safe habit?
questions.explain: any switches type checking off for everything it touches, and as only hides the problem. Data from other services crosses a trust boundary just like user input.
options: Add as Invoice so the rest of the code is typed
Assign it to unknown and parse it with a schema before use
Leave it as any; the other service is trusted

questions.q: The refund rule lives in the HTTP route handler. Later a queue consumer and an admin script also approve refunds by calling the refund service directly. What is the problem?
questions.explain: Authorization belongs where the action is, in the service layer, so every entry point goes through it. Route-level checks are fine as an extra layer, not as the only one.
options: The two new entry points skip the authorization check, because it is not in the service
The route will now reject every request

questions.q: The permission service times out while a request is being authorized. What should the handler do?
questions.explain: An authorization check that allows on error can be switched off by anyone who can make it fail, for example by overloading the permission service. Failing closed keeps the system safe while it is unavailable.
options: Allow the request, so users are not blocked
Allow it if the body says the user is an admin
Refuse it (for example with 503) and log the failure
Retry forever until the service answers

questions.q: Two support agents approve refunds on the same order at the same moment. Each request checks "amount ≤ paid − refunded" and passes, and together they refund more than was paid. Where does the final guard belong?
questions.explain: A check made before the write can be out of date by the time the write happens. The rule has to be enforced where the data changes, atomically, which is what transactions and constraints are for.
options: In the database write: a transaction that re-checks inside it, or a constraint

questions.q: What does a property-based test with fast-check add to a table of hand-written test cases?
questions.explain: You state a rule that must always hold ("a customer's request is never approved, whatever the body") and the library searches for a counterexample. It finds more than your own imagination would, but it is still testing, not proof.
options: It proves the code has no bugs
It checks a rule against hundreds of generated inputs, including shapes you did not think of, and shrinks any failure to a small example

questions.q: Why does the lesson validate GATEWAY_KEY when the service starts, instead of when the first refund needs it?
questions.explain: Failing at startup turns a configuration mistake into a failed deployment that someone notices at once, instead of a broken refund at 2 a.m. The error names the variable without printing its value.
options: Environment variables cannot be read later
A missing or malformed key then stops the service immediately and clearly, before it accepts any request

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The assertion does not change the value, so amountKobo is still the string "2500", and + with a string joins text. The compiler allowed + 100 because it believed the assertion.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: TypeScript's private is only checked by the compiler; at runtime value is a normal property and JSON.stringify includes it. The #value field is a real private field, invisible to JSON.stringify.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The template string calls toString(), and JSON.stringify calls toJSON(). Only the deliberate reveal() returns the real value, whose length is 10.

questions.q: A "finance" role was added, but the rule was not updated. What does this print?
questions.explain: ₦60,000 is above the ₦50,000 support limit, so support is denied. "finance" matches no allow rule and falls through to the final "deny": the function fails closed for the new role.
options:
support allow
manager allow
finance allow
customer deny

support deny
manager allow
finance deny
customer deny

support deny
manager allow
finance allow
customer deny

support allow
manager allow
finance deny
customer deny

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The pattern is anchored at both ends and case-sensitive, so the lowercase scheme and the token with a space do not match at all. Anything that does not match exactly is treated as "not logged in", which is the safe default.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ₦70,000 (7,000,000 kobo) is exactly what is left, so it is allowed; one kobo more is not. Zero and a fraction of a kobo fail the integer and positive checks before the business rule runs.
options: ok | 422 too much | 400 invalid amount | 400 invalid amount
422 too much | 422 too much | 400 invalid amount | 400 invalid amount
ok | 422 too much | ok | 400 invalid amount

questions.q: What does this strict check print?
questions.explain: Both role and approved are outside the allow-list. An array is an object in JavaScript, so it needs its own check. A body with only allowed keys has no unknown ones (missing required fields are a separate check).

questions.q: This is why the lesson refuses text amounts instead of converting them with Number(). What does it print?
questions.explain: Number accepts much more than digits: an empty string becomes 0, spaces are trimmed, and exponent and hexadecimal forms are understood. A strict boundary that only accepts JSON numbers avoids deciding what all of these should mean.

questions.q: An audit logger drops keys that might hold secrets. What does it print?
questions.explain: sessionToken and apiKey match the pattern (the i flag ignores case), so they are removed. A key-name filter like this is a safety net; the first defence is not putting secrets into log entries at all.

questions.q: What does this hand-written guard print?
questions.explain: Number.isInteger("500") is false, because it does not convert strings. null and arrays are rejected by the first line; without the null check, typeof null === "object" would let it through and the next line would throw.

questions.q: Which orders does each actor see?
questions.explain: Customers see only their own orders (an ownership rule); a customer with no orders sees an empty list, not everyone's. Support sees all (a role rule). In a database you would put the ownership condition into the query itself, so other customers' rows are never loaded.

questions.q: Write a Secret class that keeps its value in a private # field, returns it only from reveal(), and prints [redacted] from both toString() and toJSON(). The test code below must print the expected lines.
questions.explain: The #value field is not a property, so Object.keys finds nothing. toString covers template strings and toJSON covers JSON.stringify, which is what most loggers call.

questions.q: Write decide(actor, order, amountKobo) for refunds, deny by default. Allow only support (up to 5,000,000 kobo) and manager (any amount), never on an order whose customerId is the actor's own userId. Return "allow" or "deny".
questions.explain: The ownership rule comes first, so even a manager cannot approve their own order. The allow rules are exact matches, and everything else, including the unexpected "Manager" spelling, reaches the final "deny".

questions.q: Write parseRefund(body: unknown) without a library. It returns { ok: true, value } for an object with exactly the keys orderId (a string matching /^ORD-\d{4,10}$/) and amountKobo (a positive whole number), and { ok: false, problems } otherwise, where problems lists what is wrong. The value must be a new object, not the body.
questions.explain: This is what z.strictObject does for you: reject non-objects, report unknown keys, check each field, and build a fresh value from the checked fields only. Collecting all problems instead of stopping at the first gives the client one useful answer.

questions.q: Write actorFrom(header, sessions): accept only an Authorization header of the exact form Bearer <token>, where the token is 1 to 200 letters, digits, _ or -, and return the session's actor, or null for anything else.
questions.explain: An anchored pattern accepts one exact form and nothing else. The actor comes from the server's session map; an unknown token and every malformed header lead to the same answer: not logged in.
questions.expected:
"Bearer tok-ada" usr_ada
"Bearer tok-bola" null
"Basic tok-ada" null
"Bearer  tok-ada" null
undefined null

questions.q: A profile update may change only displayName (string, 1 to 60 characters after trimming) and phone (string of 7 to 20 digits, spaces or +). Write buildUpdate(body) that returns an object with only the valid allowed fields, or null if the body has any other key or any invalid value.
questions.explain: Every key must match a known field with a valid value; anything else refuses the whole update. The result is a new object, so it can safely be passed to a database update without carrying extra fields (mass assignment).

questions.q: Write redact(value) that returns a deep copy of a plain object or array where every property whose key matches /token|password|secret|key/i is replaced by "[redacted]", at any depth.
questions.explain: Look at the output closely: authorization does not match the pattern, so the bearer token is still logged. Key-name redaction is a safety net that misses names nobody thought of, which is why the lesson puts the protection on the value (a Secret type) and keeps headers out of logs entirely. Add authorization and cookie to the pattern in a real logger.

questions.q: Write loadConfig(env) that requires GATEWAY_URL to start with https:// and GATEWAY_KEY to be at least 32 characters. On failure it throws an Error whose message lists the names of the bad variables (comma separated) and never their values.
questions.explain: Naming the variable is enough to fix the deployment; printing the value would copy a secret into logs and error trackers. Reporting all bad variables at once saves a round of failed deploys.
questions.expected:
invalid configuration: GATEWAY_URL, GATEWAY_KEY
contains the key: false
https://payments.example
